prose.text: A tidal marsh changes character twice each day. Incoming water carries fine sediment between cordgrass stems, while the ebb leaves a thin film that dries in the sun. Ecologists place marked stakes along the creek bank and measure the ground after each spring tide. A single visit can mislead because wind and rainfall alter the result, so the useful record is a season of repeated measurements paired with weather notes.

A violin maker evaluates varnish by listening as well as looking. A hard coat can protect spruce yet damp the smallest vibrations if it becomes too thick. The maker brushes test panels cut from the same board, weighs them before and after coating, and taps each panel at several stages of curing. Color matters to the customer, but the experiment focuses on mass, flexibility, and how consistently the finish can be repaired.

The last bus through a rural valley is planned around connections rather than average speed. Its timetable leaves a deliberate pause at the rail station because the evening train is occasionally late. Dispatchers compare missed connections, passenger counts, and winter road reports before changing that pause. Removing five idle minutes looks efficient on paper, but it can strand the only travelers who have no later service.

A community seed library stores living material, so its catalogue includes more than a plant name. Volunteers record the harvest year, the garden where a variety grew, isolation precautions, and a germination test. Tomato seed may remain useful for years, whereas onion seed loses vigor quickly. Small envelopes are kept dry and cool, and older lots are planted first instead of being discarded solely because of age.

Inspectors reading an old stone bridge distinguish harmless history from active movement. Weathered mortar and rounded tool marks can remain unchanged for decades, while a fresh diagonal crack or displaced drain may signal a current load problem. They photograph fixed viewpoints, map each defect, and compare measurements after floods. The pattern over time carries more weight than the drama of a single close-up image.

During a coffee roast, beans pass through several chemical stages that cannot be judged by clock time alone. The operator watches color, listens for the first crack, and tracks the rate at which temperature rises. Dense high-altitude beans often need a different heat curve from softer beans. A useful roast log records airflow and batch mass as well as temperature, allowing the next batch to be adjusted from evidence instead of memory.

A reading room needs daylight without glare. Designers model the low winter sun, the higher summer path, and reflections from nearby windows before choosing a shade. A bright average measurement can hide uncomfortable hot spots on desks. The final design uses a pale ceiling to spread light, exterior fins to block direct rays, and small task lamps so readers can control illumination without flooding the whole room.

Divers surveying a reef cannot count every fish at once. They swim a fixed transect at a steady pace and record species crossing an imaginary belt. Visibility, current, and observer experience affect the count, so those conditions travel with the data. Repeating the same route at comparable times makes changes easier to interpret, although the method still describes the sampled corridor rather than the entire reef.

Bread dough rises because yeast produces gas inside a developing gluten network. A baker testing fermentation keeps flour, water, salt, and dough temperature constant, then changes only the rest time. Volume alone is insufficient: an overproofed loaf may look large before baking and collapse in the oven. The comparison therefore records handling strength, oven spring, crumb structure, and flavor after the loaves have cooled.

A museum label must serve a visitor who may give it only twenty seconds. Curators begin with the object and the reason it matters, then add a concrete detail that rewards closer looking. Dates and materials are checked against the catalogue, while disputed interpretations are attributed rather than stated as settled fact. The final paragraph is read aloud because long clauses that look acceptable on a screen often become awkward beside the exhibit.

An orchard on a slope can be colder at the bottom than near the ridge because dense night air drains downhill. Growers place thermometers at several elevations instead of trusting the forecast for the nearest town. When blossom temperature approaches danger, fans may mix warmer air from above, but they help only during an inversion. A windless clear night and a windy cold front require different responses even if both forecasts show the same minimum.

A navigation buoy reports a simple position but survives a complicated environment. Its mooring chain must tolerate waves, corrosion, and the changing depth of the tide without letting the buoy drift into the channel. Technicians inspect wear at the links nearest the seabed and verify the lantern from shore after dark. Position reports are compared with a surveyed reference because a light that still flashes may nevertheless have moved.

Potters learn more from witness cones than from the kiln dial. Each cone bends after receiving a particular combination of heat and time, which approximates the work done to the clay and glaze. Cones placed on several shelves reveal gradients that a single thermocouple misses. After firing, the potter records cone angle, glaze surface, and clay color, then changes shelf spacing or burner balance before altering the recipe.

Choosing a street tree begins below ground. A species that thrives in a park may fail beside traffic when its roots meet compacted soil, buried utilities, and a small planting pit. Planners compare mature canopy, drought tolerance, branch structure, and conflicts with sidewalks. They also diversify plantings, since a block filled with one species can lose all of its shade when a specialized pest arrives.

Restoring an old radio interview requires restraint. Engineers copy the original tape at a calibrated speed, keep an untouched digital master, and apply noise reduction only to a working copy. Removing every hiss can erase quiet consonants and room tone that establish the recording's character. Each edit is documented so a future listener can distinguish what the microphone captured from what the restoration process inferred.

A marker beside a glacier shows distance clearly but not cause. Researchers combine repeated position surveys with snowfall, melt, ice thickness, and flow measurements. A retreating terminus may occur while ice farther uphill still moves forward, because melting at the edge exceeds delivery of new ice. Long records help separate annual weather from a persistent change in the glacier's mass balance.

A small water system uses several barriers rather than relying on one perfect filter. The intake screen removes debris, settling reduces suspended material, filtration captures finer particles, and disinfectant controls microbes. Operators check turbidity because cloudy water can shield organisms from treatment. They also measure disinfectant at distant taps, where a good reading confirms that protection remained through the distribution pipes.

Repairing a loose book differs from making it look new. A conservator first identifies how the pages, sewing, and cover were originally joined. Reversible wheat-starch paste and compatible paper support weak areas without locking future workers into the present repair. Scuffs that document use may remain, while loose fragments are enclosed and labeled. The aim is safe handling and honest structure rather than cosmetic perfection.

A weather balloon sends a vertical profile through air that ground stations cannot sample. As it rises, its instruments measure pressure, temperature, humidity, and wind inferred from movement. The balloon eventually expands and bursts, after which a parachute lowers the package. Forecasters inspect the profile for layers, since a shallow warm inversion or a pocket of dry air can matter more than the surface reading.

A wetland boardwalk must stay usable while disturbing the site as little as possible. Designers place spans to avoid rare plants, choose piles that need limited excavation, and leave openings for water flow. The walking surface needs enough texture for rain but gaps small enough for wheels and canes. Seasonal inspections look for loose fasteners, settlement, and places where vegetation has begun to narrow the route.

Solar noon is the moment the sun crosses the local meridian, which rarely matches twelve o'clock on a civil clock. Longitude, time zones, daylight saving rules, and Earth's uneven orbital speed all contribute to the difference. A simple shadow experiment marks the shortest shadow over several minutes. Repeating it through the year reveals a smooth shift rather than an error in the clock or compass.

A beehive enters winter with a finite store of food and a cluster that moves through it. Beekeepers estimate hive mass from both sides, check that rain cannot enter, and avoid opening the box during cold weather without a reason. A warm afternoon may bring cleansing flights without indicating spring. The useful signs are sustained brood activity, food position, and the colony's ability to maintain the cluster.

A railway wheel develops a slightly conical tread so the axle can guide itself through gentle curves. When the wheelset shifts sideways, the outer wheel rolls on a larger effective diameter and travels farther per turn. Wear changes that geometry, so maintenance crews measure profile as well as obvious cracks. Reprofiling removes metal deliberately and is scheduled before the shape begins to harm ride quality or track.

A language class built for community revival has different evidence of success from a short academic course. Teachers track whether learners use greetings at home, tell stories to children, and participate in ceremonies, not merely whether they pass written quizzes. Elders decide which recordings may be shared publicly. New words for modern tools are discussed collectively so teaching expands daily use while respecting local authority.

A compost pile heats when microbes have enough moisture, oxygen, and a balanced mixture of materials. Gardeners place the thermometer in the center and turn the pile when temperature falls after an active period. Immediate reheating suggests that oxygen was limiting, while a dry pile may need water. Finished compost is judged by stable temperature, earthy smell, and the disappearance of recognizable feedstock.

Every flat world map distorts something because a sphere cannot be unfolded without stretching. A navigation chart may preserve local angles, while an equal-area map supports comparisons of land size. Cartographers choose the projection after defining the question and geographic extent. They label unusual distortion explicitly, especially when a familiar-looking map could make high-latitude regions appear more important simply because they look larger.

A theater's acoustics balance clarity with a sense of space. Early reflections from side walls help listeners locate speech, while a long reverberant tail can blur rapid dialogue. Designers test empty and occupied conditions because an audience absorbs sound. Adjustable curtains and overhead panels let one room support spoken drama and music, but measurements at many seats are needed before the controls receive their standard settings.

A rice terrace holds a shallow sheet of water on steep land by joining many small level fields. Farmers repair the bunds before planting and pass water downward through controlled openings. If one wall leaks, the damage can spread to terraces below, so inspection follows heavy rain. The system works through shared timing: an upstream decision about diversion affects every household using the same channel.

A telescope mirror is tested by observing how it redirects a known wavefront, not by judging its shine. Dust can look alarming under a flashlight yet have little effect on an image, while a subtle shape error spreads every star. Technicians record temperature because glass changes as it cools. Cleaning is postponed until contamination affects performance, since each contact with the coating carries its own risk.

An emergency drill is useful when it exposes decisions rather than rehearsing a perfect script. Observers note how quickly an alarm is recognized, whether exits remain accessible, and where people seek information. A confusing instruction is treated as evidence about the system, not as a participant's failure. The review assigns owners and dates to a small set of changes, then tests those changes in the next exercise.

import re
import unicodedata

def slugify(title):
    """Create an ASCII lowercase slug from a display title."""
    folded = unicodedata.normalize('NFKD', title)
    ascii_text = folded.encode('ascii', 'ignore').decode('ascii').lower()
    words = re.findall(r'[a-z0-9]+', ascii_text)
    return '-'.join(words)

from collections import defaultdict

def group_anagrams(words):
    """Group words by Unicode code-point multiset, preserving input order."""
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    order = []
    for word in words:
        key = tuple(sorted(word.casefold()))
        if key not in groups:
            order.append(key)
        groups[key].append(word)
    return [groups[key] for key in order]

def connected_components(graph):
    """Return sorted components of an undirected adjacency mapping."""
    remaining = set(graph)
    result = []
    while remaining:
        stack = [min(remaining)]; component = []
        while stack:
            node = stack.pop()
            if node not in remaining:
                continue
            remaining.remove(node); component.append(node)
            stack.extend(graph[node])
        result.append(sorted(component))
    return result
